Mission 1

Mission 1: Why do the French hide a charm in a January cake, and which traditions now divide them?

Make a guess: Why do the French hide a charm in a January cake, and which traditions now divide them?

Mission 1

The French calendar

  • France has 11 public holidays (les jours fériés).
  • Six are Christian in origin: Easter Monday, Ascension, Whit Monday, 15 August, 1 November (la Toussaint), Christmas. A secular Republic kept its Catholic calendar.
  • Others are civic: 1 May (la fête du Travail), 8 May and 11 November (end of the two World Wars), 14 July, 1 January.
  • 14 July (le 14 Juillet): national day by a law of 1880. It recalls the storming of the Bastille (1789) and the Fête de la Fédération (1790).
  • On the day: military parade on the Champs-Élysées, fireworks (le feu d'artifice), firefighters' dances (les bals des pompiers).
  • Watch out: un jour férié – a public holiday; faire le pont – to take the extra day off between a holiday and the weekend.
Mission 1

Customs through the year

  • January, Epiphany: la galette des rois. A small charm (la fève) is hidden inside; whoever finds it is king or queen and wears the paper crown.
  • 2 February, la Chandeleur: people make crêpes.
  • 1 April: le poisson d'avril – children stick paper fish on people's backs.
  • 1 May: people give lily of the valley (le muguet) for luck.
  • 21 June: la Fête de la musique (since 1982): free concerts in the streets.
  • 1 November: families put chrysanthemums on graves.
  • 24–25 December: le réveillon (late Christmas Eve meal), la bûche de Noël – the Yule log cake.
  • Your turn: "At Candlemas, we make pancakes."
    Show answer

    À la Chandeleur, on fait des crêpes.

?Which pair is correct?
Mission 1

Festivals across the French-speaking world

  • Québec: la Fête nationale du Québec on 24 June (la Saint-Jean-Baptiste); le Carnaval de Québec every winter since 1955, with its snowman mascot Bonhomme Carnaval.
  • Belgium: the Carnival of Binche – the Gilles dance in wax masks and throw oranges; recognised by UNESCO in 2003.
  • Switzerland: la fête de l'Escalade, Geneva (December), recalls the failed attack on the city in 1602; children smash a chocolate marmite.
  • Martinique and Guadeloupe: carnival ends on Ash Wednesday when Vaval, the carnival king figure, is burned.
  • Senegal: la Tabaski (Eid al-Adha): families gather, sacrifice and share a sheep, and wear new clothes.
Mission 1

The big cultural festivals

  • Le Festival de Cannes (since 1946, May): cinema; top prize la Palme d'or.
  • Le Festival d'Avignon (since 1947, July): theatre; founded by Jean Vilar.
  • La Fête des Lumières (Lyon, around 8 December): in 1852 people lit candles in their windows; today light shows draw huge crowds.
  • Le Carnaval de Nice (February): parades of giant figures and la bataille de fleurs – the flower battle.
  • La Fête de la musique: created by the Ministry of Culture in 1982; copied in many countries.
  • Model: Ce qui me plaît dans la Fête de la musique, c'est qu'elle est gratuite et ouverte à tous.
Quick check
?Which sentence is correct French?
Mission 1

When traditions meet laïcité

  • France's laïcité: the state is neutral towards religions.
  • Question: can a town hall display a Christmas crib (une crèche de Noël)?
  • Conseil d'État, 9 November 2016:
  • in a building housing a public authority (e.g. a town hall): not allowed, unless special circumstances give it a cultural, artistic or festive character (e.g. a local tradition);
  • in other public places (a street, a market): allowed in the Christmas period, if it does not promote a religion.
  • Some see cribs as heritage (le patrimoine, Provençal santons); others as a religious symbol that a neutral state should not display.
  • Watch out: la laïcité ≠ "laity"; it means the separation of religion and state.
Mission 1

Faut-il préserver toutes les traditions ? Argue both sides

  • Case: bullfighting (la corrida), legal only where there is an "unbroken local tradition" (parts of the south). A 2022 bill to ban it was withdrawn before it came to a vote.
  • Keep it (arguments supporters make):
  • La corrida fait partie de l'identité de certaines régions du Sud. – Bullfighting is part of the identity of some southern regions.
  • Elle fait vivre des villes entières pendant les ferias. – It supports whole towns during the ferias.
  • Ban it (arguments supporters make):
  • Une tradition ne justifie pas la souffrance d'un animal. – A tradition does not justify an animal's suffering.
  • Les traditions évoluent : on peut fêter une région sans mise à mort. – Traditions change: a region can celebrate without a killing.
  • Linkers: Au nom de la tradition, … · Pour les uns …, pour les autres … · Tout dépend de …
  • Your turn: "For some it is an art; for others it is cruelty."
    Show answer

    Pour les uns, c'est un art ; pour les autres, c'est de la cruauté.

Mission 1

Vocabulary bank and model sentences

  • une fête – a celebration, festival · un jour férié · une coutume – a custom · célébrer / fêter · un défilé – a parade · le feu d'artifice · un char – a float · se déguiser – to dress up · une tradition qui se perd – a dying tradition · le patrimoine immatériel – intangible heritage · la marchandisation – commercialisation · transmettre – to hand down
  • Même si la pratique religieuse recule, beaucoup de fêtes religieuses restent des moments familiaux.
  • Si les fêtes locales disparaissaient, une partie de l'identité régionale disparaîtrait avec elles. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • Ce qui rend une fête vivante, c'est qu'elle se transmet d'une génération à l'autre. (cleft for emphasis)

Mission 2

Mission 2: More than one person in ten in France is an immigrant. Who came, when, and what did they bring?

Make a guess: More than one person in ten in France is an immigrant. Who came, when, and what did they bring?

Mission 2

Who counts as an immigrant?

  • INSEE (France's statistics office): un immigré = a person born abroad as a foreigner who lives in France.
  • Once an immigrant, always counted as one, even after becoming French.
  • un étranger = a person without French nationality (some were born in France).
  • un descendant d'immigrés = born in France with at least one immigrant parent. Not an immigrant.
  • 2025 (provisional): 8.0 million immigrants = 11.6% of the population.
  • One in three (33%) has become French.
  • Born in Africa: 49%; born in Europe: 30%.
  • Top countries of birth: Algeria (12.6%), Morocco (11.7%), Portugal (7.2%), Tunisia, Italy, Turkey, Spain.
  • Watch out: un émigré = someone who left a country. Les immigrés arrivent, les émigrés partent.
Quick check
?Sofia was born in Lyon to Portuguese parents and has Portuguese nationality only. How does INSEE classify her?
Mission 2

Waves of immigration

  • 19th century: France's birth rate is low; industry needs workers. Belgians (northern mills), Italians (south-east).
  • 1920s: after the First World War's losses, Poles for the coal mines of the North; Italians; Armenians after the 1915 genocide; Russians after the revolution.
  • 1939: about half a million Spanish Republicans cross the Pyrenees (la Retirada).
  • 1945–1974, les Trente Glorieuses: reconstruction and growth. Workers from Italy, Spain, then Portugal, Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, West Africa.
  • Many live in shanty towns (les bidonvilles, e.g. Nanterre) until the 1970s.
  • 1962: about a million rapatriés (pieds-noirs) and harkis arrive from Algeria. They are French, not counted as immigrants.
  • 1974: economic crisis; the government suspends labour immigration.
  • 1976: family reunification (le regroupement familial) allows workers' families to join them.
  • Late 1970s: refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
  • Since the 1990s: more varied origins; students, skilled workers, asylum seekers; Ukrainians since 2022.
Mission 2

Why people came: push and pull

  • les facteurs d'attraction – pull factors: jobs, wages, family, studies, safety, the French language.
  • les facteurs de répulsion – push factors: poverty, war, persecution, dictatorship.
  • fuir la guerre / la misère – to flee war / poverty
  • chercher du travail – to look for work
  • rejoindre sa famille – to join one's family
  • demander l'asile – to apply for asylum; un réfugié – a refugee
  • s'installer en France – to settle in France
  • Your turn: why did Spanish Republicans come in 1939?
    Show answer

    Ils ont fui la guerre civile et la dictature de Franco.

  • Watch out: fuir is irregular: ils fuient (present), ils ont fui (perfect), ils fuyaient (imperfect).
Quick check
?Why is 1974 a turning point in French immigration history?
Mission 2

Contributions: the economy

  • Immigrants rebuilt France after 1945: mines, steel, building sites, car factories (e.g. Renault at Boulogne-Billancourt).
  • Today many work in sectors short of staff: building, care for the elderly, cleaning, hotels and restaurants, farming.
  • Many hospital doctors trained abroad, often outside the EU.
  • Immigrants also set up businesses: shops, restaurants, start-ups.
  • Economists debate the net effect on public finances: most studies find it small, positive or negative depending on the method.
  • Useful phrases:
  • Les immigrés occupent souvent des emplois pénibles et mal payés. – Immigrants often do hard, badly paid jobs.
  • Ils contribuent à l'économie en travaillant, en consommant et en payant des impôts. – They contribute by working, spending and paying taxes. (en + present participle)
Mission 2

Contributions: culture, science, sport

  • Science: Marie Curie, born in Warsaw, Nobel Prizes in 1903 (physics) and 1911 (chemistry).
  • Literature: Romain Gary (born in Vilnius); Leïla Slimani (born in Rabat, prix Goncourt 2016).
  • Art: Picasso and Chagall worked in France for decades; Chagall became French in 1937.
  • Song: Yves Montand (born in Italy); Aya Nakamura (born in Bamako, Mali).
  • Sport: the 1998 World Cup team was celebrated as black-blanc-beur; Zinedine Zidane, born in Marseille to Algerian parents, is a descendant of immigrants.
  • Food and language: couscous is an everyday French dish; words such as toubib (doctor) and kif come from Arabic.
  • Since 2007 the Musée national de l'histoire de l'immigration (Palais de la Porte Dorée, Paris) tells this story.

Mission 2

Vocabulary bank

  • une vague d'immigration – a wave of immigration
  • la main-d'œuvre – the workforce, labour
  • un travailleur immigré – an immigrant worker
  • le pays d'origine / d'accueil – country of origin / host country
  • la terre d'accueil – land of welcome
  • le regroupement familial – family reunification
  • un demandeur d'asile – an asylum seeker
  • un sans-papiers – an undocumented migrant
  • obtenir la nationalité française – to become a French citizen
  • la mixité – (social, ethnic) mix
  • enrichir / l'enrichissement – to enrich / enrichment
  • un apport – a contribution
Mission 2

L'immigration, une chance pour la France ? Argue both sides

  • Arguments supporters make:
  • L'immigration comble les pénuries de main-d'œuvre. – It fills labour shortages.
  • Face au vieillissement de la population, la France a besoin de jeunes actifs. – With an ageing population, France needs young workers.
  • La diversité enrichit la culture française. – Diversity enriches French culture.
  • Arguments critics make:
  • L'immigration pèse sur le logement et les services publics. – It puts pressure on housing and public services.
  • Elle peut tirer les salaires vers le bas dans les emplois peu qualifiés. – It can push down wages in low-skilled jobs.
  • La France devrait choisir ses immigrés selon ses besoins. – France should choose its immigrants according to its needs.
  • Balance: Il ne s'agit pas de savoir si …, mais comment … – The question is not whether …, but how …
  • Policy debates by party: see another lesson.
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "Without immigrant workers, France would not have been rebuilt so quickly."

Exam tasks

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • 11 public holidays; 14 July national day since 1880; customs: galette des rois, Chandeleur, muguet, Fête de la musique (1982).
  • Francophone festivals: Québec (24 June, winter carnival), Binche, l'Escalade, Antilles carnival, Tabaski.
  • Debates: cribs and laïcité (Conseil d'État 2016); bullfighting, tradition or cruelty.

Mission 2

  • Immigré (born abroad as a foreigner) ≠ étranger (not French) ≠ descendant d'immigrés (born in France).
  • 8.0 million immigrants (11.6%) in 2025; top origins Algeria, Morocco, Portugal.
  • Waves: industry (19th c.), 1920s, Trente Glorieuses, 1974 stop, 1976 family reunification. Contributions in the economy, science, arts, sport and food.
